w10_P4_001594: An engineering team is testing a magnetic rail launcher that fires small research sleds down a horizontal track. During a firing, the sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 3t^2 + 5t, where t is the time in seconds after the coils switch on. The team needs the speed the sled has gained between t = 1 second and t = 2 seconds, and that speed becomes the release speed of a 14 kilogram sled at the end of the track. (The launch rail itself is 6.0 meters long, a fact that plays no role in what follows.) They need the energy this sled carries because of that release speed, first in joules and then expressed in kilojoules. Taking that kilojoule figure, they multiply it by 11, subtract 13 from the result, and then multiply what remains by 8. What is this final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001599: A machinist has two brass rods, one 28 centimeters long and the other 321 centimeters long, and wants to cut both into equal-length pieces with nothing left over, using the longest piece length that works for both. Whatever that greatest piece length turns out to be, in centimeters, she multiplies it by 5 to get the acceleration, in meters per second squared, that a press ram must undergo. The ram itself has a mass of 87,000 grams. Find the net push the press must exert to give the ram that acceleration, first in newtons and then in kilonewtons. Take that kilonewton figure, multiply it by 7, and then subtract 11 from the result. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001600: A test rig runs 5 identical trials on a spring-loaded launcher. In each trial, the launcher combines a baseline push worth 5 units with an extra boost worth 11 units, and the results from all 5 trials are added together to give the total speed, in meters per second, imparted to a small cart. That speed sends a cart with a mass of 4,000 grams down the track. Find the energy this cart carries because of that speed, in joules. Take that number, subtract 18, then add 29 to what remains, then multiply the result by 11, and finally express that amount in kilojoules. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001608: At a hydraulic press testing bench, the ram's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 4t^2 + t during the power stroke, where t is the time in seconds after the pump engages. Engineers need the speed gained by the ram between t = 0 and t = 3 seconds. That speed is reached by a 46 kilogram ram head. (The bench's hydraulic reservoir holds 15 liters of fluid, which plays no role in this calculation.) Find the energy the ram head carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 12, then subtract 6 from the result. Convert what remains into kilojoules, and then add 12 more to that figure. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001612: The number a crane-hoist inspector finally writes down, in kilonewtons, is 13 more than a value obtained by multiplying an intermediate force reading by 6. That intermediate reading, in turn, is 21 more than a force -- expressed first in newtons, then converted to kilonewtons -- that a 174,000 gram hoist counterweight exerts while undergoing a certain acceleration. That acceleration, in meters per second squared, is the smaller of two candidate readings from the hoist's calibration log: two numbers that add up to 9 and multiply together to give 14. What is the final number the inspector writes down, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001617: The figure a drone-rotor engineer reports, in kilonewtons, comes from converting a force measured in newtons -- a force that is 28 less than an earlier reading. That earlier reading is the net push a 71 kilogram rotor housing exerts while undergoing an acceleration equal to 17 more than the rotor arm's instantaneous speed at a certain moment. That speed, in meters per second, is how fast a point on the arm is moving at t = 3 seconds, given that its position along the arm, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 - 6t^2 for t in seconds since the motor starts. What is the final figure, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001621: A quality inspector at a component test bench has 7 identical-looking capacitors on a tray and needs to select 2 of them at random to install in a test circuit. The number of different pairs she could possibly choose becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, applied to a small test carriage with a mass of 160 kilograms. Find the push this carriage requires to reach that acceleration, in newtons. Take that number and multiply it by 2, then multiply the result by 9, then by 9 again, and then by 9 one more time. What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001622: The number a conveyor-belt technician ultimately records, in newtons, is 27 more than an earlier figure. That earlier figure is itself 15 more than a force reading, taken in newtons, after that force was multiplied by 3. The unmultiplied force is what a 73 kilogram gearbox housing exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to 5 times the total acceleration gained by a test slider between t = 0 and t = 2 seconds, where the rate at which the slider's own acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 4t^2 + t over that interval. (The gearbox housing is bolted to a base plate that is 1.8 meters wide, which plays no role here.) What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001625: At a robotics lab, a technician must choose 4 servo motors out of a batch of 8 identical units to install on a new arm. The number of different groups of 4 she could form becomes the speed, in meters per second, of a 36 kilogram test arm swinging freely. (The lab bench is 1.4 meters wide, which plays no role in this calculation.) Find the energy this arm carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 20 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, then multiply it by 2, and then multiply the result by 8. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001627: The final number a wind-turbine test engineer logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier kilojoule figure by 11, after that figure was already multiplied by 7. Before either of those multiplications, that number was the energy -- first found in joules, then converted to kilojoules -- carried by a 50 kilogram nacelle test mass moving at a certain speed. That speed, in meters per second, is 8 more than the speed gained by a component between t = 1 second and t = 3 seconds, given that its acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 2t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001630: The number a catapult test crew finally reports, in kilonewtons, is 29 more than a force reading that was originally measured in newtons before being converted. That force is what a 21 kilogram counterweight arm exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to 5 times the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 267 centimeter cable and a 379 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001632: A packaging line runs 4 short production cycles. On cycle k (for k = 1, 2, 3, and 4), the line adds exactly k extra boxes to a pallet beyond its base load; adding up the extra boxes from all 4 cycles gives a total, which the line operator multiplies by 2 to get the speed, in meters per second, of a small transfer cart carrying a 12 kilogram tray. (The pallet itself is stacked 1.5 meters high, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this cart carries at that speed, in joules, and express that amount in kilojoules. Multiply the result by 12. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001635: A calibration sheet for a flywheel test rig lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a spinning test mass: the two numbers add up to 12 and multiply together to give 35. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. Multiplying that speed by 2 gives the actual launch speed of a 54 kilogram flywheel segment. Find the energy this segment carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 2 as well. Convert what results into kilojoules, and then add 18 to that figure. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001638: The number a go-kart pit crew ultimately writes on the sheet, in newtons, is 21 less than an earlier figure. That earlier figure is itself 26 less than a force reading, in newtons, after that reading was multiplied by 6. The unmultiplied force is what a 102 kilogram kart chassis exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the larger of two candidate readings on the calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 13 and multiply together to give 40. (The kart's fuel tank holds 5 liters, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001643: The number an escalator-motor technician finally reports, in kilonewtons, is 9 more than an earlier kilonewton figure after that figure was multiplied by 3. Before that, the value was a force -- first found in newtons, then converted to kilonewtons -- that a 173 kilogram gearbox exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to 6 times the total acceleration gained by a test shaft between t = 2 seconds and t = 3 seconds, given that the rate at which the shaft's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = t^2 + t over that interval. (The escalator step belt is 0.9 meters wide, which plays no role in this calculation.) What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001649: At a piston test cylinder, the rate at which the piston's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 3t^2 + 2t, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the total acceleration the piston gains between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds. That acceleration is applied to a piston head with a mass of 132,000 grams. Find the push this piston head requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Subtract 29 from the result, and then multiply what remains by 8. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001650: A calibration log at a car-engine test rig lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a piston assembly: the two numbers add up to 7 and multiply together to give 12. The correct reading is confirmed to be the larger of the two. That acceleration acts on a piston assembly with a mass of 82,000 grams. (The test rig's cooling loop circulates 3 liters of coolant, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the push this assembly requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Subtract 22 from the result, multiply what remains by 5, and then subtract 12 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001659: The number a centrifuge-rotor technician finally logs, in kilojoules, is 26 less than an earlier figure, which is itself 14 more than a kilojoule reading obtained by converting an energy value from joules. That joule value is the energy carried by a 54,000 gram rotor segment moving at a certain speed, after that energy was multiplied by 6. The speed itself, in meters per second, is the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 50 centimeter cable and a 129 centimeter cable on the rig, with nothing left over. (The rotor housing is cooled by a fan drawing 40 watts, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001660: A robotics technician must pick 2 sensors out of 10 identical units on a shelf for a new test batch. The number of different pairs she could form becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a test carriage with a mass of 155,000 grams. Find the push this carriage requires to reach that acceleration, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Add 4 to the result, and then multiply what remains by 9. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001663: The number a roller-coaster launch-cart engineer finally writes down, in joules, is 3 less than an earlier figure. That earlier figure is itself 28 more than a value that was, before that, 7 more than an energy reading, in joules, after that reading was multiplied by 8. The unmultiplied energy is what a 34 kilogram launch cart carries while moving at a certain speed. That speed, in meters per second, is how fast a point on the cart's guide arm is moving at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 for t in seconds since release. (The guide arm itself is 4.5 meters long, a fact that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in joules?
w10_P4_001665: At a wind-tunnel model test bench, the model's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 3t^2 + t, where t is the time in seconds after the tunnel fan reaches speed. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds. That speed is reached by a scale model with a mass of 23,000 grams. Find the energy this model carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 13 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, multiply the result by 7, and then add 10 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001670: At a crane-hoist facility, technicians run 12 successive lift cycles. On cycle k (for k = 1 through 12), the hoist motor adds exactly k extra kilograms of load beyond its base test weight; adding up the extra load from all 12 cycles gives a total, which becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a counterweight with a mass of 41,000 grams. Find the push this counterweight requires, in newtons, then add 16 to that number. Convert what results into kilonewtons, multiply by 8, and then multiply the result by 7. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001674: At a pinball launcher test rig, the rate at which the plunger's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 2t^2 + 4t, where t is the time in seconds after release. Engineers need the total acceleration gained between t = 0 and t = 1 second. That acceleration acts on a plunger head with a mass of 25 kilograms. Find the push this plunger head requires, in newtons, then subtract 26 from that number. Multiply what remains by 12, then by 5, and then convert the result into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001675: At a skateboard ramp test lab, a technician repeats a push-off test 3 times. Each run combines a baseline push worth 2 units with an extra kick worth 10 units, and adding the results from all 3 runs together gives the total speed, in meters per second, of a rider model. That speed applies to a rider model with a mass of 21,000 grams. (The ramp itself is 4 meters tall, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this model carries at that speed, in joules, then add 22 to that number, then add 8 more. Convert what results into kilojoules, and then add 14 to that figure. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001677: At a gear test bench, two steel shafts measure 63 millimeters and 193 millimeters across their keyways. A technician wants the greatest length, in millimeters, that divides evenly into both measurements with nothing left over, and that greatest length becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a test gear with a mass of 42,000 grams. Find the push this gear requires, in newtons, then add 4 to that number, then add 22 more. Multiply what remains by 6. What is the final number, in newtons?
